title: Xueyan Feng
text:
I study how people judge messages when AI takes part in writing or selecting them. My research asks how AI involvement changes what a message signals about its sender, and which messages reach the public.
I am a master’s student in Integrated Marketing Communications at Northwestern University (M.S. expected December 2026). At Northwestern, I work with Professor Edward C. Malthouse on how large language models (LLMs) recommend brands, and with Professor Chao Yu on how restaurants’ replies to online reviews changed after ChatGPT and on AI note writers on X’s Community Notes. I hold a B.A. in Korean Language and Literature from Peking University.
Research interests: AI-mediated communication · gatekeeping on platforms and by AI · computational communication

title: Research
text: Generative AI now writes messages matched to a recipient at minimal human effort, and it increasingly helps decide which messages people read. My projects take up both sides of this change. The first asks what a message still signals about its sender when AI helps write it. The second asks how AI changes gatekeeping, the process that reduces countless pieces of information to the few messages that reach the public.

title: Research
text:
What AI-assisted messages signal

Accommodation made cheap: AI and restaurants’ replies to online reviews
With Chao Yu (Northwestern University) and Wang Liao (University of Washington)

Question. How did restaurants’ public replies to online reviews change after ChatGPT, and does tailoring a reply to the review still set it apart? The study draws on communication accommodation theory and signaling theory.
Data and methods. 8.9 million reviews and 487,906 replies on OpenTable across six U.S. metro areas. Interrupted time series with restaurant and period fixed effects; tailoring is measured as how closely a reply resembles the review it answers.
Findings. Compared with before 2023, replies took up their reviews far more closely, most of all in quarters when AI likely wrote at least half of a restaurant’s replies. More tailored replies went with more later reviews before 2023 but no longer did from 2023. The data cannot yet attribute that change to AI authorship.
Status. Extended abstract submitted to ICA 2027.

title: Research
section: Gatekeeping on platforms and by AI
text:
Gatekeeping on platforms and by AI

Diminishing returns to AI note writers: Human raters limit what Community Notes publish
First author, with Chao Yu (Northwestern University)

Question. On X’s Community Notes, a note is published only when raters with differing perspectives rate it helpful. AI programs now write notes too, but only humans rate them. Do AI note writers increase what the platform publishes? The study draws on gatekeeping theory.
Data and methods. 791,143 notes flagging posts as misleading, from the first AI note in September 2025 to September 2026. Time-series and fixed-effects models.
Findings. Ratings tracked human-written notes, not AI-written ones. When AI output doubled, each AI note received 10% fewer ratings and was 12% less likely to be published. AI writers scaled up note production far more than the human ratings that decide which notes are published.
Status. First-author extended abstract submitted to ICA 2027.



The Silent Gatekeeper: Brand visibility in LLM recommendations
With Edward C. Malthouse, Jing Yang, Sanchary Pal, and Kun-Yu Lee

Question. How often and how prominently do LLMs recommend brands to consumers seeking product advice? The study treats LLMs as gatekeepers between consumers and brands.
Data and methods. A measurement framework that estimates recommendation prevalence (Brand Recommendation Probability) and prominence (an adapted Mean Reciprocal Rank) from repeated queries. Multiple LLMs, five product categories, and needs-based prompts; models were queried through their APIs in new sessions with no conversation history. Regularized regression on marketplace-visibility measures.
Findings. Many major brands were rarely or never recommended. Recommendation prominence was associated with marketplace visibility, particularly search interest and online brand conversation.
Status. Revise and resubmit, Journal of Advertising Research. A related paper is submitted to ECIR 2027 (arXiv:2609.16304).



The machine brand image: Evaluating LLM recommendations across prompts and models
With Jing Yang, Kun-Yu Lee, Sanchary Pal, and Edward C. Malthouse

Question. When LLMs recommend brands, they also explain why. The study treats these justifications as brand associations.
Data and methods. 17,821 justifications from six LLMs across five product categories, coded into eight association types and linked to marketplace data.
Findings. The associations mirrored brands’ positioning and were largely shared across LLMs. A consumer’s stated need shifted them from reputation toward situational fit.
Status. Competitive paper accepted at AAA 2027; submitted to Journal of Advertising.



In progress: How an LLM’s knowledge of the consumer shapes brand recommendations
With Edward C. Malthouse, Jing Yang, Sanchary Pal, and Kun-Yu Lee

Design. Compares a stateless model, the user’s own LLM personalization, and a synthetic persona, with participants querying their own AI assistants. I designed the participant survey and ran the factor analysis.
Status. Paper in preparation for ICORIA 2027.

title: Research
text:
Next steps
Observational data can narrow the explanations for these patterns but not choose among them. Signaling theory predicts that a message loses value once AI makes it cheap to produce; communication accommodation theory treats adapting to one another as a persistent tendency of human communication. I plan online experiments that vary whether AI involvement is disclosed, who sends the message, and whether it is private or masspersonal (written for one person yet readable by anyone), to test when each prediction holds.
